question: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine checkup. He has had a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He does not have a fever or any discharge from the swelling. He underwent a colectomy for colon cancer at the age of 43 years. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. Current medications include insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen. He has worked as a traffic warden for the past 6 years and frequently plays golf. He appears healthy. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 130/86 mm Hg. Examination of the neck shows a 2.5-cm (1-in) firm, mobile, and painless nodule. The skin over the nodule cannot be pinched. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A photograph of the lesion is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Insulin glargine -> treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus -> helps regulate blood glucose levels -> 80% CHAIN: Type 2 diabetes mellitus -> increased risk of developing lipomas -> possible association -> 70% CHAIN: Lipoma -> benign tumor composed of fat cells -> common in middle-aged adults -> consistent with patient's age -> 90% CHAIN: Firm, mobile, painless nodule on the neck -> characteristic of lipoma presentation -> fits clinical findings -> 85% CHAIN: Lipoma -> most likely diagnosis for the patient's neck nodule -> supported by clinical features -> 80%
analysis: Based on the clinical presentation of a painless, firm, mobile nodule on the nape of the neck without any signs of inflammation or discharge, along with the patient's medical history and the appearance of the lesion, the most likely diagnosis is a lipoma. Lipomas are common benign tumors composed of adipose tissue that are typically soft, mobile, and painless. The lack of skin pinch over the nodule is also characteristic of a lipoma.
